finding.claim: The /fetch2 endpoint fetches any http(s) URL the client supplies. The only check is the scheme, so a caller can reach internal hosts, loopback, and cloud metadata endpoints such as http://169.254.169.254/. Redirects are followed by default, which adds a second path to internal targets. This is full SSRF.
finding.sink: requests.get(url, timeout=5) with redirects enabled; the first 200 characters of the response body are returned to the caller

trace.note: is_http_url only checks that the scheme is http or https, with no host or IP check
requests.get(url, ...) runs with the default allow_redirects=True, and the response body is returned

finding.guards_checked: is_http_url checks the scheme only. There is no host or IP filtering, no allowlist, and no redirect restriction. No authentication decorator is present.

verdict.guard_found: none (is_http_url at validators.py:7 is a scheme-only check; no auth decorator, no host/IP filter, no redirect restriction)
verdict.reason: views.py:19-22 passes the attacker-controlled `url` query parameter to requests.get with default redirects after only the scheme-only check at validators.py:7, so internal hosts and metadata endpoints are reachable. The safe variant `is_safe_url` and `allow_redirects=False` are used only on /fetch (views.py:12-14), not /fetch2.

finding.claim: The /fetch endpoint blocks private, loopback, link-local and reserved IPs, and disables redirects. The check is vulnerable to DNS rebinding (TOCTOU). is_safe_url resolves the hostname once, and requests.get resolves it again independently. An attacker-controlled DNS server can answer with a public IP for the first lookup and an internal IP (e.g. 169.254.169.254 or 127.0.0.1) for the second. The request then goes to the internal host. This is lower confidence than finding 1 because it needs a DNS server the attacker controls and a short-TTL race.
finding.source: request.args.get('url'), with an attacker-controlled hostname whose DNS answers change between lookups
finding.sink: requests.get(url, timeout=5, allow_redirects=False), whose body is returned to the caller

trace.note: socket.getaddrinfo resolves the hostname for validation only; the result is discarded
Rejects private, loopback, link-local and reserved IPs from that first resolution
requests.get(url) resolves the hostname again and connects to whatever IP that second lookup returns

finding.guards_checked: The scheme is restricted to http/https. All resolved addresses are checked against private, loopback, link-local and reserved ranges. Redirects are disabled, which closes the redirect bypass. The resolved IP is not pinned for the actual connection, which is the gap. Also, getaddrinfo is called with port parsed.port or 443 even for http URLs; this has no security effect.

verdict.guard_found: Scheme restriction plus a one-time getaddrinfo IP-range check (validators.py:12-17). It is not a closing guard: the resolved IP is not pinned and requests.get resolves again.
verdict.reason: validators.py:14 resolves the hostname only to validate and discards the result, then views.py:14 calls requests.get(url) on the attacker-supplied URL, which resolves it a second time. A rebinding DNS server can therefore return a public IP first and an internal IP second.
